scenes.tts: The first film followed a receptor as it loaded a G protein. If an empty receptor already signals, where can a ligand move the response?
scenes.caption: The first film followed a receptor as it loaded a G protein. If an empty receptor already signals, where can a ligand move the response?
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's membrane and color map exactly: receptor blue, ligand gold, G-alpha purple, beta-gamma teal, GDP gray, GTP green. An empty blue receptor flickers gently beside a large vertical meter labeled 'schematic response'. The meter already sits above zero. Three dashed destinations appear above, at, and below its current level, each marked with a question.
scenes.narration: The first film followed a receptor as it loaded a G protein. If an empty receptor already signals, where can a ligand move the response?

scenes.visual: Hold the question in large type. The empty receptor continues flickering between less-active and more-active cartoons. The meter trembles around its starting level, and the three possible destinations pulse without revealing labels.
Show 'Above, At, or Below Basal' over the same membrane and meter for two seconds. Keep ambient receptor flicker behind the title, then remove only the title.

scenes.tts: A receptor population can signal even when every binding pocket is empty. Individual receptors sample less-active and more-active shapes. If some active shapes engage G proteins, the population produces basal activity. That starting signal becomes the reference for classifying what a ligand does.
scenes.caption: A receptor population can signal even when every binding pocket is empty. Individual receptors sample less-active and more-active shapes. If some active shapes engage G proteins, the population produces basal activity. That starting signal becomes the reference for classifying what a ligand does.
scenes.visual: Expand to a row of six large blue receptor cartoons, all with empty pockets. They flicker independently between closed and open cytoplasmic faces. Each open face briefly nudges a purple G-alpha block. Their combined pulses feed the response meter, which settles on a dashed line labeled 'basal activity'. Keep 'schematic response' visible.
scenes.narration: A receptor population can signal even when every binding pocket is empty. Individual receptors sample less-active and more-active shapes. If some active shapes engage G proteins, the population produces basal activity. That starting signal becomes the reference for classifying what a ligand does.

scenes.tts: An agonist raises signaling above that line. In the simple picture, it favors the more-active receptor population. Gold agonist blocks settle into open receptor pockets. More receptors remain signaling-competent, so the meter rises. Agonist describes the measured effect, not merely the ability to bind.
scenes.caption: An agonist raises signaling above that line. In the simple picture, it favors the more-active receptor population. Gold agonist blocks settle into open receptor pockets. scenes.visual: Carry the same receptor row and meter. Gold ligand blocks descend into the pockets of more-active receptors. Closed cartoons transform toward the open cytoplasmic shape, never into molecular structures. Receptor-to-G-protein pulses become more frequent. The meter rises above the dashed basal line, and the destination gains the label 'agonist'.
scenes.narration: An agonist raises signaling above that line. In the simple picture, it favors the more-active receptor population. Gold agonist blocks settle into open receptor pockets. More receptors remain signaling-competent, so the meter rises. Agonist describes the measured effect, not merely the ability to bind.

scenes.tts: A neutral antagonist behaves differently. By itself, it leaves basal signaling approximately unchanged. Its job appears when another ligand arrives. Antagonist blocks occupy the pockets, so the incoming agonist finds few free receptors. At this agonist dose, the meter stays near basal instead of rising. Neutral describes the drug's effect on basal activity.

scenes.visual: Reset every receptor and the meter to basal before changing the label. White-edged neutral-antagonist blocks (a color not used elsewhere in the map) occupy both less-active and more-active receptor pockets without shifting their mix. Gold agonist blocks approach; most bounce from occupied pockets and drift away, and one finds a free pocket. The response meter stays near the dashed basal line. Label the state 'neutral antagonist'.
scenes.narration: A neutral antagonist behaves differently. By itself, it leaves basal signaling approximately unchanged. Its job appears when another ligand arrives. scenes.tts: An inverse agonist moves the response below basal. In the simple picture, it favors the less-active receptor population. Red-edged ligand blocks settle into those receptors. Fewer receptors engage G proteins, and the meter falls. The prefix inverse refers to signaling direction, not to opposite binding.
scenes.caption: An inverse agonist moves the response below basal. In the simple picture, it favors the less-active receptor population. Red-edged ligand blocks settle into those receptors. Fewer receptors engage G proteins, and the meter falls. The prefix inverse refers to signaling direction, not to opposite binding.
scenes.visual: Reset to the unliganded basal row first. Red-edged inverse-agonist blocks enter less-active pockets. More receptor cartoons close their cytoplasmic faces, receptor-to-G-protein pulses become rare, and the meter slides below the basal line. Label the destination 'inverse agonist' only after the fall is visible.
scenes.narration: An inverse agonist moves the response below basal. In the simple picture, it favors the less-active receptor population. Red-edged ligand blocks settle into those receptors. Fewer receptors engage G proteins, and the meter falls. The prefix inverse refers to signaling direction, not to opposite binding.

scenes.tts: Now remove measurable basal activity from the assay. The meter starts at zero. A neutral antagonist cannot lower it. Neither can an inverse agonist reveal a further decrease. Added alone, they look the same. Distinguishing them requires a receptor system with a visible basal signal.

scenes.visual: Transform the meter into a matched assay panel with its baseline at zero. Show the neutral-antagonist condition on the left and inverse-agonist condition on the right. In both, occupied receptors sit above identical zero readings. A bracket joins the two readings with 'indistinguishable here'. Do not label either drug as ineffective or rejected.

scenes.tts: Real ligands can produce intermediate changes, even at a saturating concentration. Carazolol, bound in inactive beta-adrenergic receptor structures, is a partial inverse agonist. In an assay, it lowers basal signaling without producing the full reduction possible there. Efficacy means the response a bound ligand can produce. Partial describes its efficacy in that measured pathway, not incomplete binding in this assay.
scenes.caption: Real ligands can produce intermediate changes, even at a saturating concentration. Carazolol, bound in inactive β2-adrenergic receptor structures, is a partial inverse agonist. In an assay, it lowers basal signaling without producing the full reduction possible there. Efficacy means the response a bound ligand can produce. Partial describes its efficacy in that measured pathway, not incomplete binding in this assay.
scenes.visual: Carry the below-basal meter into a comparison with two schematic inverse-agonist conditions. The first reaches a lower endpoint; the carazolol condition stops partway between basal and that endpoint. Label the carazolol ligand on screen and mark its receptor 'beta-2'. Do not draw a chemical structure or imply a universal maximum. A bracket labels the smaller measured change 'partial efficacy'.
scenes.narration: Real ligands can produce intermediate changes, even at a saturating concentration. Carazolol, bound in inactive β2-adrenergic receptor structures, is a partial inverse agonist. In an assay, it lowers basal signaling without producing the full reduction possible there. Efficacy means the response a bound ligand can produce. Partial describes its efficacy in that measured pathway, not incomplete binding in this assay.

scenes.tts: The active-versus-inactive picture is a useful first model, not a claim of only two rigid structures. Receptors sample ensembles of shapes. Efficacy is measured for one response in one cell. A ligand classed in one assay may class differently in another. Keep the meter and assay beside the receptor whenever you name efficacy.

scenes.visual: Let each blue receptor cartoon soften into several overlapping blue outlines labeled 'ensemble', all explicitly schematic. Keep the same ligand and show two side-by-side response meters labeled 'measured response A' and 'measured response B', without inventing different numerical results. A frame encloses receptor, ligand, assay, and meter as one classification context.

scenes.tts: Use one reference line and three questions. Does the ligand raise signaling above basal? Does it leave basal unchanged while blocking another ligand? Or does it lower signaling below basal? Those observations separate agonism, neutral antagonism, and inverse agonism without pretending the receptor is a simple switch.

scenes.visual: Return to one large schematic response meter with a bright basal line. Animate three clean paths from the line: up to 'agonist', level with an incoming ligand blocked to 'neutral antagonist', and down to 'inverse agonist'. The same blue receptor population remains beside every path. Fade all objects before the end card.
